subtype: Stage 2: Cutting contact to protect herself [Actor]
passage: I'm Himani, and it's been eight months since I last picked up when Mummy called. At first it was survival. Every call after the wedding went the same way: what kind of daughter does this, what will people say, look at your cousin Pallavi, she listened to us. I'd hang up shaking and couldn't work for the rest of the day. So one Sunday I let it ring. Then again. The quiet felt like air. My counsellor says that break may have been what I needed. But now I notice something else. When Pallavi texted last week that Mummy has been unwell, my thumb hovered over Mummy's number and just... didn't move. Not answering has become a groove I don't know how to climb out of.

qa.q: How long has it been since Himani last picked up when Mummy called?
qa.a: It has been eight months since she last picked up.

qa.q: What does Himani's thumb hovering without moving suggest about her feelings?
qa.a: Part of her wants to reach out to her unwell mother, but old hurt and the habit of silence hold her back; she feels stuck.

qa.q: What small step could help Himani climb out of the groove without returning to painful calls?
qa.a: She could send a short text on her own terms, such as asking how Mummy is, and keep limits like ending a call if criticism starts.

qa.q: How might Mummy experience eight months of unanswered calls?
qa.a: She may feel hurt, rejected and anxious, and perhaps still not see how painful her own words were for Himani.

grounding: A young woman looks back on stopping her mother's critical calls as a needed break that has since become a hard-to-undo habit.

subtype: Stage 2: Cutting contact to protect herself [Actor]
passage:
Session note, Ganga, counsellor. Third session with Shabnam.
Shabnam said her father has called every evening since her wedding, and every call ends with him listing her mistakes. Three weeks ago she stopped answering. She described the first silent week as 'finally being able to breathe', and her shoulders dropped as she said it.
Today she also said, more quietly, that now even a message from her brother makes her put the phone face down. She laughed, but her hands were twisting her sleeve.
My thoughts: the break has protected her. The risk is that avoidance spreads and sets into a habit she can't easily reverse.
Plan: help her decide, in her own time, which contacts feel safe, and practise how to end a call when criticism starts.

qa.q: How did Shabnam describe the first silent week?
qa.a: She described it as 'finally being able to breathe'.

qa.q: What does Shabnam twisting her sleeve while laughing suggest?
qa.a: Her laugh hides unease; she seems worried that avoiding contact is spreading further than she intended.

qa.q: What turning point does the counsellor's plan offer?
qa.a: Choosing which contacts feel safe and practising how to end a call when criticism starts gives Shabnam protection without letting silence set into a permanent habit.

qa.q: What might Shabnam's brother feel when his messages go unanswered?
qa.a: He may feel confused and shut out, even though he wasn't the one criticising her.

grounding: A counsellor notes a young woman who stopped answering her father's critical calls: the break helped, but avoidance is starting to become a habit.

passage:
The nurses' station on Ward 6 was quiet at two in the morning. Zainab's phone buzzed on the counter. Ammi. Again.
Tejas glanced at it. "You're not going to take it?"
"It's the fourth call today. She'll say I've shamed the family. Then Abbu will take the phone and say it louder." She turned it face down.
"How long have you not answered?"
"Six weeks." Zainab straightened a file that didn't need straightening. "At first it was a break. I could finally sleep. Now..." She shrugged. "Now I don't know how to start again."
The phone buzzed once more, then stopped.

qa.q: How long has Zainab not answered?
qa.a: Six weeks.

qa.q: What was Zainab feeling as she straightened a file that didn't need it?
qa.a: She seemed uneasy and hurt, relieved to escape the criticism but troubled that not answering has become hard to undo.

qa.q: What turning point could Zainab consider at this stage?
qa.a: Choosing a safer way to reconnect, such as a short message with limits, rather than letting silence become permanent.

qa.q: How might Ammi be experiencing the unanswered calls?
qa.a: She may feel frightened and hurt by the silence, even as her calls keep pushing Zainab further away.

grounding: Shows a young woman who stopped answering her parents' painful calls, first as a break and now as a hard-to-undo habit.

subtype: Stage 2: Cutting contact to protect herself [Actor]
passage:
Hi Mehak,
You asked why I haven't mentioned my mother lately. I stopped picking up in January.
Every call was the same. Why did I marry him, when will I leave that job, look how old I look in photos. I would sit on the stairs afterwards, shaking. So one day I just let it ring. Then again. It felt like finally taking a breath.
But here's what scares me. It's April now. Last week it was her birthday, and I didn't call. I didn't even decide not to. I just didn't. The silence has become a habit, and I'm not sure I know how to break it, or if I want to.
Can we talk this weekend?
Gopika

qa.q: When did Gopika stop picking up?
qa.a: In January.

qa.q: How can you tell Gopika is both relieved and worried?
qa.a: She says not answering felt like finally taking a breath, but she is scared that the silence has become a habit she can't break.

qa.q: What small step could help Gopika at this stage?
qa.a: Talking it through with Mehak and perhaps a counsellor, so she can decide calmly whether and how to reconnect.

qa.q: What might Gopika's mother be feeling on her birthday with no call?
qa.a: She may feel hurt and bewildered, perhaps not seeing how her criticism led to the silence.

grounding: Shows a young woman who stopped answering painful calls from her mother, finding relief but fearing the silence has become a habit.

subtype: Stage 2: Cutting contact to protect herself [Actor]
passage:
So, Divyansh, you asked on the drive what happened with my parents. Okay. After the wedding, they called every Sunday. Every Sunday, the same list. My husband's job, my clothes, when their daughter would come to her senses. I'd cry in the car after.
One Sunday I just didn't pick up. Then the next. I felt so light, I can't tell you. Like someone lifted a sack off my back.
That was eight months ago. Now Sunday comes and I don't even check who's called. It's just what I do. And sometimes I wonder, if Amma called to say sorry, would I even know? That's the part that scares me. I'm Usha. I did what I needed to, and I'm still not sure it's finished.

qa.q: How long ago did Usha stop picking up?
qa.a: Eight months ago.

qa.q: What was Usha feeling when she first stopped answering?
qa.a: She felt light and relieved, as if a heavy sack had been lifted from her back.

qa.q: What turning point is available to Usha now?
qa.a: She could check her messages occasionally or set a boundary for calls, so the break stays a choice rather than an automatic habit.

qa.q: How might Divyansh see Usha's story?
qa.a: Divyansh may feel sympathy for the painful calls and also understand her worry that the silence has become fixed.

grounding: Shows a young woman who stopped answering hurtful weekly calls, felt relief, and now fears the break has become a habit.

subtype: Stage 2: Cutting contact to protect herself [Actor]
passage:
March. Ammi called every evening at eight. Every call circled back to the same place: "You've shamed us. People ask about your husband's family." Farida would hang up shaking and sit on the kitchen floor. Her flatmate Nandini made tea and said nothing.
May. Farida stopped answering. The phone buzzed at eight, then stopped. The evenings grew quiet. She slept better. "It's a break," she told Nandini. "I need to breathe." Nandini agreed.
November. The calls came less often now, once a week, then not at all for a month. Farida noticed she no longer even looked at the screen. On Eid she typed "Eid Mubarak, Ammi", stared at it for ten minutes and deleted it. Not answering had become easier than answering, and that frightened her more than any call ever had.

qa.q: What time did Ammi call every evening in March?
qa.a: Ammi called every evening at eight.

qa.q: Why did Farida feel frightened on Eid?
qa.a: She felt frightened and sad to realise that not answering had become a habit, easier than reaching out even with a simple greeting.

qa.q: What could Farida do at this stage to keep the break from hardening into permanent silence?
qa.a: She could send a short, safe message like the Eid greeting, or set her own limits for a call, so the distance stays a choice rather than a habit.

qa.q: What might Nandini be seeing as the months pass?
qa.a: Nandini sees Farida go from shaking after calls to sleeping better, and may also notice the quiet turning into something harder to undo.

grounding: Shows a young woman stopping answering painful calls as a needed break, and the silence slowly becoming a habit that is hard to undo.
